layers.title: In the browser
layers.lede: Everything anyone using the tool does: read the design, set the inputs, run, keep what a run returned. **Nothing in the browser changes the design.** What you set and what you keep are yours and stay on your machine; what the design *is* changes only in its owners' own files, sealed as each group's release and taken into today's design from the shared drive.

sections.title: Open the tool
sections.answer: Start the tool with one command and open the address it prints. It never writes the repository: what you keep — the case and your results — stays on your machine under ~/.vleo.
sections.body:
The tool is one program on your own machine. It serves this page and computes every number on it, from one address, with no internet and no database. It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so nobody else on the network can reach it.

**It never writes the repository.** The two things you can keep — the case you run on and the results you save — are kept outside it, under `~/.vleo/`, so a checkout stays exactly as it was released and `git status` is empty however much you use the tool. The status card at the top of this manual says where this copy keeps them.

steps.say: Start it. It prints the address it got — the first free port from 7777 upward.
Open the address it printed, normally `http://127.0.0.1:7777`.
In a Codespace there is nothing to type: the tool is already running and port 7777 opens as a preview.

Without a repository, the tool comes two ways. The one file for every laptop: `python -m pip install vleo-<version>-py3-none-any.whl` once, then `python -m vleo` — it runs inside Python, so Windows has no new program to stop. Or a kit, the zip for your system: double-click `Start VLEO.exe` on Windows, or run `./start.sh` on macOS and Linux. Either opens the page itself; `START_HERE.md` says the rest.

sections.title: Who does what
sections.answer: Five roles. The programme manager, the system engineer, each subsystem engineer and each node engineer own the design and use the tool; a group's work reaches the design as its sealed release, put on the shared drive, where the tool takes it into today's design when it opens. The developer maintains the code and releases the tool — and writes what no routine can: code, checks, the tool itself. Each role has a deputy who may act for it.
sections.body:
The line between the roles is the line between *owning and using* the design, *moving a change through*, and *building the machinery*. The design's own roles follow the tree: the **programme manager** owns the management side, the **system engineer** the whole spacecraft and the one release everyone works from, each **subsystem engineer** their group's branch, and each **node engineer** their nodes (`docs/OPERATING_1_0.md`, section 2).

**Everyone uses it.** Anyone can set the inputs — by hand or as a CSV — run any row on them, save what the run returned and send it on, and look at a result somebody else saved without running anything. When a node is wrong, missing or unfinished, its node engineer — the person who knows the answer — changes it in the node's own file, and their subsystem engineer seals the group's work as a **release** and sends it.

**A sealed release goes on the shared drive**, in its group's `releases/` folder. When the tool opens on the drive it builds today's design from every group's latest sealed release that passes its checks — its seal, its content, each node against the design — and says which release each group's part is, and why one was refused. Nobody takes a release in by hand. From the switch-over on, each owner signs their own files in the application, and the developer maintains only the code.

**The developer builds the machinery.** A method that needs maths the kernel does not have needs code in the kernel; a check that fails for a reason not in the release needs a diagnosis; the tool's pages, pictures, checks and generators are designed and improved. All of it through the gate and a reviewed pull request.

There are three guides — for the engineers, `docs/roles/user.html`; for the releases until the switch-over, `maintainer.html`; and for the developer, `developer.html` — generated from this manual, so the three can never disagree with it.

sections.title: Find your way around
sections.answer: The design is a tree of rows in four layers, drawn with its connections on one grid. Pick a layer, open a group, click a row to open its page.
sections.body:
The design is a tree of rows in four layers. Each row asks one small question and has one answer. The tabs across the top are the layers, plus the architecture every row repeats.

The big figure shows two things on one grid. The **tree** runs down the diagonal: a group is a box, a row is a cell. The **connections** are the marks: a row's own row of the grid is what it feeds, its column is what feeds it. Click anything and its inputs light up one colour and what it feeds another.

From the keyboard: the **up** and **down** arrows move the selection, **left** and **right** open and close a group, **Esc** goes back to the layer.

sections.title: Read a row
sections.answer: A row's page opens with its answer first, then says it simply, then the real relation and its source, then where the simple version breaks. Every claim says whether it is sourced, derived or declared, and the depth switch chooses how much is shown.
sections.body:
A row's page answers four questions, in order.

**What it is made of** — what its node file holds, which part a person writes (the sheet, with its method and cases) and what is rendered from it.

**What it is joined to** — the rows it reads, the rows that read it, and which customer targets it feeds.

**What it says** — the sheet itself, laid out the same way on every row: an **Answer first** box, then the row **said simply**, then **the real thing** — its relation and where that came from — then **where the simple version breaks**, and the wrong idea readers most often bring. Every claim is marked *sourced*, *derived* or *declared*, and every tab says whether it is an explanation, a reference or something to try. The **de-risking** tab says what the row rests on and why it changed.

**The picture** — for the rows that have one, the figure the claim is argued from.

A **grey** row is *seeded*: it exists and nothing is specified in it yet. That is the normal state of most of the tree — the decomposition written down before anyone was asked to fill it — not a failure; its node engineer fills it. A row marked **INACTIVE** has a relation but nothing on its sheet saying where the relation came from, so it does not answer until its node engineer supplies that.

sections.title: Set the inputs — the case
sections.answer: Every run is on one case: its inputs, set on the Inputs page or uploaded as a CSV and saved outside the repository. A file is shown before it is saved, refused whole if any row is bad, and carried over when the tool is updated.
sections.body:
There is **one case**, the multipayload design, and every run, sweep and figure in the tool is for it. What changes from one customer to the next, or from one sky to the next, is its **inputs** — never the tree. A customer is a set of values, not a folder, so a new customer is never a change to the design.

The **Inputs** tab lists all of them in two halves. **Condition** is what the design flies in: the orbit, the environment and the solar weather it is sized for. **Customer** is everything else — the payloads, the vehicle, the service and what it must deliver. Each shows the value it runs at, its default — the value declared on its own sheet — and the range it may move in.

Change values there and save them, or **upload a CSV**. A file is read and shown before anything is saved: what it sets, what that changes, and every row it refuses. A file with any refused row — a name that is not an input, a unit that is not the row's, a value outside the declared range — is not used at all, because keeping the good half would be a run on values nobody asked for. A blank value means the default, so a file only has to name what it changes.

The saved case is kept by the tool **outside the repository** — beside the reference data, in `~/.vleo/case/`, or wherever `VLEO_CASE` points — so git never sees it. To keep a copy, or hand one to someone, download it; to put it back, upload it. The bar across the top always says how many inputs the saved case changes.

**When the tool is updated, a case carries over.** Every CSV the tool writes names the set of inputs it was written for, in a `#! template` line — keep it. When a release adds, retires or re-ranges inputs, a case written before is not refused: every value that still applies is carried, every new input runs at its default, and any value that can no longer be used — its input retired, or now outside its range — is **set aside** by name, with its value and why, rather than dropped. The saved case is carried over on its own the first time the updated tool reads it, and the file as it was is kept beside it; the Inputs page says what the update did until you keep the result. An old file you upload is carried over the same way, and shown before it is saved.

sections.title: Run a row, and ask “what if”
sections.answer: Run any computed row on the case, or change an input first to ask what if. A run always says how many rows ran and names every one that was blocked.
sections.body:
Every computed row can be evaluated on the spot, on its own page or from the **4 The run** tab.

**A run is on the case** — its saved inputs, see *Set the inputs*. The panel says so in a sentence, and under it lists every input the answer depends on, the most influential first, each with the value it will run at, which half of the case it is in, and where the value came from: the **default**, the **saved case**, or **your edit**.

**Change one to ask a what-if.** The edit is kept in this browser only — listed in the bar at the top, applied to every run and sweep until you reset it, and never written to a file. A **computed** row cannot be changed this way: its value would be recomputed from its inputs the moment it ran, so change one of the declared numbers it reads instead. When a what-if is worth keeping, **save it to the case** and every page runs on it from then on.

The result always says **n ran, m blocked**, and names every blocked row. A row with nothing in it does not quietly supply a default — it refuses, under its own name, and everything that needed it says so. That count is never hidden, because a number built partly on refusals is not the number it looks like. What unblocks such a row is its node engineer's answer, taken in with the group's release — see *What comes in from outside, and what does not*.

sections.title: Keep a result, send it, and see it again without running
sections.answer: Save a run or a sweep as a result, and see it again later without running anything — or send its report page. A question already answered is not run again: the tool shows the saved answer and says so. A result keeps the node versions it rested on, and says when one of those beliefs has broken since.
sections.body:
A run is worth keeping when somebody will ask about it later. **Save** it and the tool keeps a **folder**: `result.csv` — every value the run returned with its unit, its credibility and what governs it, every row it blocked on and why, and **every input it ran on** — `sweep.csv` when it is a sweep, and `report.html`, the page to send. It is kept in `~/.vleo/results/` or wherever `VLEO_RESULTS` points — outside the repository, like the case.

**A question already answered is not run again.** Everything that decides an answer — the row, how much of the graph, every input, the engine, the tree and the reference data, and for a sweep what it moved and how — is one key. Press **run** or **sweep** on a question already kept and the saved answer is shown, with a line saying which result it came from and when; **run again anyway** runs it fresh. Saving the same question twice keeps it once. With `VLEO_RESULTS` on a shared folder, that includes questions a colleague answered. A change to the engine's code or to the tree is a different key, so an answer from before a correction is never shown for the corrected tool.

The **Results** tab lists every saved result and shows any of them as it was — **nothing runs**, so a result saved before a release reads exactly the same after it. Two results can be compared value by value, and the inputs that differ between them are listed first, because that is usually the answer.

A saved **sweep** is drawn again on the Results page from its saved points, with the same chart the run panel uses — hover, zoom and copy the numbers — and nothing runs.

To send one, download its **report**: one HTML page that reads without the tool, draws the sweep, and carries the CSVs inside it, so uploading the report gives the result back whole. The **CSV** opens in any spreadsheet. A result somebody sent you is uploaded the same way: its report, or its `result.csv` with its `sweep.csv`.

**Results are kept in tiers.** Every value for 30 days — `VLEO_KEEP_DAYS` sets how many — and the summary for good: when the tool starts, an older result is thinned to the inputs it ran on, its answer and what could not run, and says so on its page and in its report. The rest is one run away, because the same engine on the same inputs gives the same answer; a thinned result is not offered as a kept answer, so asking its question again runs it. **Pin** a result to keep every value of it for good. A shared folder named by `VLEO_RESULTS` is kept whole unless `VLEO_KEEP_DAYS` is set too.

**A result's inputs can become the case.** That puts every input back to what the result ran on — the way to reproduce it, or to carry on from it. It is checked like any other case, and refused whole if a release has since retired or re-ranged something it sets.

sections.title: What comes in from outside, and what does not
sections.answer: Two things reach the tool from outside: your inputs, and a result you kept. Neither changes the design. A node changes only in its own file, written by its node engineer and sealed in its group's release.
sections.body:
The **Forms** page lists both, with where each is set: the inputs on the Inputs page, as a CSV or one value at a time, and results on the Results page, shown without running. Both are yours, kept on this machine.

**A node is not among them.** What a node asks, how it computes and what it reads is the design, and the design is written by the people who own it, each in their own file. A group's work reaches this tool as its sealed release, on the shared drive. The browser never writes a node.

**A lesson is the one thing still filled here**: a row's lesson form, filled anywhere and checked as you type, sent back to the developer.

sections.title: Why a node changes — its beliefs, versions and risks
sections.answer: A node changes only because a belief it rested on broke, and every change records what we believed, what we tested, what we now know and what changed. The risk-register rows of the management layer conclude, from every node's record, how that work has moved the programme's risks.
sections.body:
Every decision in the design rests on a belief — that this relation holds here, that this input is the one that matters, that this picture shows what it claims. A node changes only when one of those beliefs **breaks**: somebody tested it and learned otherwise. So a node's page has a **de-risking** tab. It says what the node rests on now and what would break it, then every version before it, newest first: what we believed, what we tested, what we now know, what it cost, what changed, and which risks that moved.

`sw_central_expectation` — the centre of the F10.7 design value — carries its real history as the worked example: three versions, each replaced because a test showed its belief did not hold.

**The conclusion is drawn in the management layer.** A risk is registered once, on one of the four risk-register rows — technical, schedule, supply, regulatory — and moved only by node versions. Each of those rows' pages lists its risks, where each started and where it stands now, and every version across the tree that moved it. That is how the work below, taken together, has de-risked the programme; `docs/DERISK_NARRATIVE.md` is the same thing as a document, and `docs/derisking.csv` as a spreadsheet.

**A saved result keeps the versions it rested on.** When one of those rows has moved on since, the result says so beside its number.

**How deep a page goes is yours to choose.** The switch at the top — **Learn**, **Read**, **Expert** — shows the same pages at three depths: Learn keeps every step and asks you to predict before you run; Read shows the answer, the plain words and the real thing; Expert keeps the answer, the relation, the limits and the reference. How every page is laid out, and why, is in `docs/EXPLAINING.md`.

sections.title: What the browser will not do
sections.answer: The browser never changes the design. Each thing it will not do has a place it is done instead, and for anyone using it that place is almost always the node's own file, written by its node engineer.
sections.body:
The browser never changes the design: not a field, not a row, not the tree. That is not to keep anybody out. A change to the design has to be checked against every row that reads it, implemented, given evidence, and released so that everyone runs the same thing — and a change typed into one copy of the tool does none of that. So each one below has a place it is done instead, and for anyone using it that place is almost always the node's own file, taken in with its group's release.

The fields a group's release cannot change — the ones that move a row in the tree or change who owns it — are listed live under *Reference*, each with its reason.

layers.title: Maintaining the repository
layers.lede: The routine that moves the tool to everyone's copy: build a node from its method, cut a release, build the kits, pack the drive, share. **Every step is one command**, and each does its whole step or nothing and says what to do next. Nothing here writes code — what needs code goes to a developer, with the output that says why.

sections.title: Check a node's method against its node engineer's cases
sections.answer: Run method with the node's id. It checks the method and runs every one of the node engineer's cases through it — the same check the node engineer saw in the group's application, and the one the gate refuses on.
sections.body: The gate refuses a node whose method does not check, whose cases disagree, or that has fewer than three answers and one refusal. A case that disagrees is the node engineer's to settle — their code, their method or their expected value is wrong — so it goes back to them with the line printed, never to a tolerance.

sections.title: Check a node against its cases
sections.answer: A node is built from its method in its group's application, and arrives in the group's sealed release. Here, method checks one node's method on its node engineer's cases, and rerun runs the node engineer's own code on them again.
sections.body:
Nothing here writes a node. Its group writes it, checks it and seals it in the application (`docs/GROUP_APPS.md`); what the repository holds is `design/`, the design as its files, and every case it holds must pass on the engine that reads it — each fixture, each node engineer's case, the properties from each declared range and each prior implementation's grid.

A case that fails is the node engineer's to settle. It is never a tolerance to change.

sections.title: Release a version
sections.answer: Once maintainer and developer are merged into main, run ship on an up-to-date main. Merge the pull request it opens the way to and tag the merge commit; the release pipeline builds and publishes the four files itself.
sections.body:
`ship` cuts `release/<version>`: the de-risking narrative regenerated, every node version still marked `next` stamped with this release, regeneration, the gate, the tests, one commit, pushed.

**The merge is the decision.** The release workflow builds only a commit that a merged pull request put on main, and refuses anything else before it builds (docs/RELEASE_SETUP.md). After the merge, tag the merge commit (the commands `ship` prints). The **release** workflow then builds the three kits and the one-file package, installs the package on Windows, macOS and Linux, and publishes the release with the four files attached; share the `.whl` with everyone.

Choosing the number: the middle number for new behaviour or a change in how everyone gets the tool, the last for fixes.

sections.title: What goes to a developer
sections.answer: Anything that needs code or judgement about the machinery: a method that needs a relation the kernel does not have, a check that fails for a reason of its own, a merge conflict, a change to the tool itself. Hand over the command and its output.
sections.body:
**A new relation.** A node whose method calls on maths the kernel does not have needs a function in `vleo-core::physics` first — a developer's step, and a reviewed change every node reads.

**A failing check.** The gate or a test fails for a reason in a node, a generator or the pipeline. The output names it; hand it over with the branch.

**A merge conflict** in the code.

**The tool itself** — its pages and pictures, the commands in this layer, the checks, the release pipeline. Those are code, reviewed as code.

layers.lede: Paste these from the top of the repository. Each command is marked with what it does: the ones marked **safe to run** only read, and the pipeline runs every one of them exactly as written here and holds it to what this page says it prints. The ones marked **changes files** are not run by the pipeline — they would change the repository it is checking — but their names and flags are still checked against the programs themselves.

sections.answer: Install Rust, clone, wire the hooks once and fill the reference-data store once. Then the gate and the tests are the one command that must be green.

The only thing to install is Rust; the exact version is pinned in `rust-toolchain.toml` and fetched on first use. There is no database and no service.

`setup` points git at the project's own hooks so the commit-message rule runs before a bad message ever leaves your machine. Git will not do this on its own, because a hook that ran just because it was cloned would be a way to run anybody's code.

Every command here is written out in full. Two shorter forms work too: `cargo xtask …` for `cargo run -p xtask -- …`, and `cargo vleo …` for `cargo run -p vleo-cli --bin vleo -- …`.

sections.title: Run, change an input, sweep, keep the result
sections.answer: Run a row on the case, on a CSV of your own or on the declared defaults, change a declared input with --set, sweep one, and keep a run as a result file.
sections.body:
The examples use the storm row `sw_ap_design`: *what daily Ap is this design built to survive?* It reads one declared number, the storm level designed for, and turns it into the Ap that level bounds.

A run prints the answer, its **credibility** — the weakest of eight factors, named — and **n ran, m blocked** with every blocked row named. The **chain** hash identifies that exact number: the engine, the tree and every input that reached it. Two runs with the same chain are the same run, so it is the thing to quote.

A run is on the **case**: the saved one — the same file the browser saves — or, with `--inputs`, a CSV of your own, or with `--defaults` every input at its declared value. The first lines of a run say which. `vleo inputs` prints the case as a CSV to fill in; a blank value means the default, and a file with any row that cannot be applied is refused whole, each bad row named. A file written by an older version of the tool — its `#! template` line says so — is carried over instead, and `vleo inputs --inputs old.csv` writes it out in the current template, with every value it could not carry kept as a `#! set-aside` line. The order is fixed: each row's declared value, then the case's, then `--set`.

`--set` only changes a **declared** number — never a computed one, which would be overwritten the moment it was evaluated — and it never writes the sheet.

`--save` writes the run as a **result** file where you say; `--keep` keeps it in the results folder the browser's Results page shows, once. A question already kept there is shown from its saved result instead of run — the first line says so — and `--again` runs it anyway. `vleo result` shows a result again, from its folder, its CSV or its report, without running anything.

Two of the steps use a **closure**, `l3_solar_ach_01`: the room the sustained F10.7 requirement has left once the design flux is taken from it. The launch date is one of the declared numbers behind it, and a time is given in seconds.

sections.title: Check a node — the developer's reading of it
sections.answer: The developer never writes a node. To see where one stands: check its method against its node engineer's cases, gate it, and ask whether a person should look yet. Every step names exactly what is still open.
sections.body:
A node is written, checked and sealed by its group, in the application, and reaches this repository only in `design/` (`docs/GROUP_APPS.md`). Its relation is its **method**, run by the interpreter; there is no code to write for it.

What the developer can do is read it: check its method on its cases, run the gate on it, and ask whether a person should look yet. Something the code cannot yet do comes back as a **request** (W14), and is answered with an application release.

**No assistant may supply the relation.** The method comes from its node engineer, and a person's name goes against it.

steps.say: Check the row's method, every line and every unit, and run it on each of its node engineer's cases.
Check it. Every failure names the field and the rule.

sections.title: Record why it changed, and cut a release
sections.answer: Every change to what a node computes appends a version to its node; the narrative is regenerated from all of them; and an application release sets the application's version, never the design's.
sections.body:
A change that moves what a node computes carries its reason — what we believed, what we tested, what we now know, what changed, and what the node rests on now. The node engineer writes that record in the application, with the change, and the library refuses a change to what a node computes that carries none. A risk move names a risk registered on a risk-register row, or the record is refused.

The narrative is generated from every node's record: `docs/DERISK_NARRATIVE.md` to read and `docs/derisking.csv` for a spreadsheet, in the columns of the quarterly de-risking narrative. The pipeline regenerates both and fails on a difference.

An application release names its own version. `xtask release <version>` sets the workspace version and regenerates; the release pipeline runs `release <version> --check` and refuses while the workspace says another. It stamps nothing in the design: which release carried a belief is said by the design's own release. Why, and the rules, are in `docs/DERISKING.md`.

A saved result says which node versions it rests on — and, if one has moved on since, that a belief it rested on has broken.

sections.title: What a command does, where it stopped, and why a node is what it is
sections.answer: Every xtask command is described in one table: explain prints a command's place in a node's journey, what it reads, writes and checks, how to undo it and where its code is. A command that writes prints numbered steps, says why it stopped and how to retry, leaves a trace, and takes --dry-run. why puts a node's history in one place.
sections.body:
**One table describes every command** — `xtask/src/pipeline.rs`. `explain` prints it for one command, or the whole journey with none; `docs/PIPELINE.md` is the same table as a page, regenerated by `xtask pipeline`; and a test fails when the table, `help` and the code disagree.

**A command that writes runs as numbered steps** — `release` and `ship`. Each step prints `n/total · name` as it starts and what it found when it ends. A step that stops prints **why**, the state the **files** are in, the exact command to **retry**, and the **code**: the file, and the step's name — a string in that file, so searching for the printed name finds the line.

**Every such run leaves a trace** in `target/xtask-trace/` — the command line, the commit, each step with its time and result. `xtask trace` shows the last one, `trace <command>` the last of one command, `trace --list` every one kept (the newest 50).

**--dry-run, on any command that writes**, does nothing: it runs the command's own check where it has one (`release --check`, `method-wasm --check`, `pipeline --check`), and otherwise prints the plan — its steps, what it would write, how to undo it.

**why <node>** answers "how did this node come to be this?": every recorded version and who made it, the commits that changed it, how its code came to be, and its gate, run now.

steps.say: The whole journey, and the command at each step.
One command: where it sits, what it reads, writes and checks, how to undo it, and where its code is.
What a command would do, doing nothing.
A node's history in one place, and its gate now.

sections.title: Work on the page without the engine, and change what they share
sections.answer: The page and the engine meet at one contract in contract/: every route, a schema for every answer, the file formats, and answers recorded from the real engine. A frontend developer runs the page on the mock engine with no Rust; a backend developer proves the engine keeps the contract with cargo test. Inside /v1 a change may only add.
sections.body:
**The contract is `contract/`** — `routes.toml` lists every route and the requests the tests make; `schemas/` has one schema per kind of answer; `formats/` the CSV files people keep and send; `examples/` answers recorded from the real engine. `contract/README.md` is the whole of it.

**The backend keeps it.** The contract tests start the real server and make every request: every answer must validate against its schema, and a field the schema does not declare is a failure — so the page may read only what the contract lists. They run in `cargo test`.

**The frontend builds against it.** `tools/mock_engine.py` serves the page from `web/` and every answer from the recorded examples, with no Rust built; the page says **MOCK ENGINE** at the top, because every number on it is an example. `tools/mock_check.py` walks the page on it in a browser, and the pipeline runs that with no Rust toolchain at all.

**Changing it.** Within `/v1`, add only: a new route or field breaks nobody. A field goes into the schema first, in a pull request both sides review; then either side can use it. Removing or re-meaning one is `/v2`, beside `/v1` for a release. When an answer's shape changes, re-record the examples. The page carries the contract version it was built for and names an engine that speaks another.

steps.say: The mock engine checks itself: every recorded example reads, and each request finds the answer it should.
The page on recorded answers, with no Rust — then open the address it prints.
Re-record the examples from the real engine after an answer's shape changes. A schema is never rewritten: that is the contract, changed by hand.

**The form** is one HTML file — from `lesson form`, or *write a lesson — its form* on the row's page. It carries the method checker the pages carry, which holds the lesson check the gate runs, and a table of the tree's rows, so a widget naming a row that is not there is refused while the node engineer types. **lesson check** says what a filled one holds and every reason it would be refused. sections.title: Share the tool with everyone
sections.answer: Everyone gets the tool, not the repository: one Python package for every laptop, or a kit per platform — the programs beside exactly the files they read, with START_HERE.md on top. They use it and send back node forms; you apply them, release, and share the next version.

Zip it and share it. A kit runs on the platform that built it; the release pipeline builds one for Linux, macOS and Windows, and one Python package, `vleo-<version>-py3-none-any.whl`, that carries the engine for every system and runs with `python -m vleo` — no new program for Windows or an antivirus to question. Each person's case and results live under `~/.vleo/`, outside both, so the next version replaces them without losing either. The whole loop is in `docs/SHARING.md`.

sections.title: The method language and the pages' checker
sections.answer: The method language is one module, vleo_sheet::method. The pages that check a method carry it compiled to WebAssembly as web/method.wasm.gz; after changing the language, rebuild that file with method-wasm and commit it with its stamp.
sections.body: The gate, the library and every page that checks a method call `vleo_sheet::method` — the pages through `web/method.wasm.gz`, which `xtask method-wasm` builds from `crates/vleo-method-wasm`. A test refuses a checkout whose checker sources have moved on from the committed file, so a page can never check by older rules than the gate. A page reads the file from beside the tree when it is made; no program carries it built in, because compressed WebAssembly inside a program is what Chrome blocked in the first 0.3.0 Windows kit, and the release refuses a program that does. `docs/PSEUDOCODE.md` is written by `xtask docs` from the same tables the checker reads. sections.title: When the method language cannot say it
sections.answer: A node the method language cannot express has no relation until the language can say it. It stays open, refused by name if a run reaches it, and what it needs is a request to the developer.
sections.body:
The language is closed on purpose: every construct has one meaning, so the interpreter needs no judgement. A relation it cannot express is not written in code instead: the node stays an open block, refused by name, and its node engineer raises a request with the evidence. The developer answers it by growing the language — and no assistant supplies the relation, the method or a case.

When the language grows a construct, it grows in `crates/vleo-sheet/src/method.rs` and the files under `method/` beside it — the grammar (`parse.rs`), the checker (`check.rs`) and the interpreter (`run.rs`) together, one reviewed change, followed by `method-wasm` so every page checks by the new rules.

sections.title: Is the evidence real?
sections.answer: Two commands ask whether the evidence is worth anything: every fixture declaration is sound, and every case the design holds passes on the engine that reads it.
sections.body: A test that passes against a broken implementation is not testing anything. Two commands ask that question directly.

The pipeline runs all of these on every push; running them first saves a round trip. The first is the one that must be green.

Commit messages read `type(scope): a sentence saying what changed`. The hook installed by `setup` refuses anything else before it leaves your machine, and the pipeline runs the same rule. A change that came from a group's release names who sealed it. How many reviewers a change needs is in `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

Once merged, the change reaches everyone in the next release: they update, and their saved case carries over on its own — see *Set the inputs*.

sections.title: When something goes wrong
sections.answer: The usual failures, each with what it means and what to do. Almost every refusal names the field and the rule, and that line is usually the whole answer.
sections.body:
**The tool will not start: nothing was free.** It tries sixteen ports from 7777 upward. Something else is holding them — often an earlier copy of the tool. Stop that one, or set `VLEO_PORT` to start somewhere else.

**An uploaded case or result is refused.** Every refused row is named, with why. A case is all or nothing, so correct the named rows and upload it again. A file from an older release is carried over rather than refused; one the tool did not write — no `#! result` line — is not a result at all.

**A group's release is refused on the drive.** Today's design names the group, the release and why — an input naming a row that does not exist or one of a different quantity, a broken seal, an assistant's method — and builds that group's part from its last good release. The fix goes back to the group.

**The checks refuse a row.** Each failure names the field and the rule. Read that line before anything else; it is almost always the whole answer.

**A row prints INACTIVE and does not answer.** Its relation is written but nobody has derived it: the sheet has no `[theory]` block saying why it is this relation. That is a person's work, supplied by the node's engineer, never something to work around — and every row that reads it is blocked, by name, until it is done. `active` lists each such row and how many rows wait on it.

**A sweep answers no point.** Every point is still recorded, with why: *blocked* when a row on its chain does not answer, or the bound and its reason when the value is outside the declared range of the row being swept.

**A command warns that the hooks are not wired.** Run `setup` once in this checkout.

**The commit hook refuses a message.** It must read `type(scope): a sentence`, and `tools/commit_message.py --types` prints every type and scope it accepts.

**A number looks wrong.** Run the row in the terminal, read its credibility line and which factor governs it, and look at *the chain behind this number* — every value that reached it, with each one's own credibility. If the design is what is wrong, that goes to the node's engineer.

layers.title: The codebase
layers.lede: What is in the repository, why each part is there, and what breaks without it.

sections.title: The shape of it
sections.answer: One kernel computes every number; everything else is arranged in rings that depend inward only. A row is one file in design/, and nothing in the repository writes it.
sections.body:
**One kernel computes every number.** Everything else is arranged in rings that depend inward only: quantities and portable maths (`vleo-units`), then the kernel of physics and relations (`vleo-core`), then transport (`vleo-bus`), then the engine that runs the design read from its files (`vleo-modules`), then the faces — the browser daemon, the command line, and the Python, WebAssembly and C bindings. `xtask graph` checks every dependency points inward.

**Every formula lives in `vleo-core::physics` and nowhere else.** A row composes relations from there in a few lines; it never defines one of its own.

**The tree is layers of rows.** Layer 1 is the programme's view, layer 2 the system's, layer 3 the subsystems', and layer 4 is a run. Each subsystem reaches the layer above through exactly one interface row, so *where did this number come from* is answered by walking upward without ever leaving the tree.

**One row is one file**, `design/groups/<group>/nodes/<row>.vnode`:

its block, ports and wires — what it asks, reads and returns, and from where.
its test cases — known-good values from outside this code.
its texts — the row's method, its explanations, and the sheet it was converted from.
Nothing in the repository writes it, and no row holds code: its method is run by the interpreter.
The row's page is not in the file: the tool renders it from the sheet when it is opened.

The rules that do not bend, and the developer's loop, are in `AGENTS.md`; the reasoning behind the architecture is in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`.

sections.answer: Every folder and file at the top of the repository, and what it holds — checked against the repository both ways.

commands.name: sheet
commands.what: Each node's sheet as the design holds it, as JSON by id: the text every reader of a sheet reads, for a tool outside the program to read through the one reader.

commands.name: why
commands.what: A node's history in one place: every recorded version and who made it, the commits that changed it, how its code came to be, and its gate, run now.

commands.name: trace
commands.what: The last run's trace from target/xtask-trace/ — every command that writes leaves one, the newest 50 kept — or the last of one command, or --list every one kept.

commands.name: pipeline
commands.what: Write docs/PIPELINE.md from the pipeline table; --check only says whether it is current.

commands.name: ship
commands.what: Cuts a release from main on its own branch `release/<version>`: the de-risking narrative, the version stamp, regeneration, the gate and the tests, one commit, pushed — and prints the tag commands for after the merge.

commands.name: readers
commands.what: The docs folder for readers: every row's page — the tool's own generated page — and every lesson, read with no tool running, from a shared drive or an internal web server. A lesson's widgets are answered by the engine compiled for the browser (crates/vleo-kernel-wasm), run on the design the folder carries — the tree converted to its files, opened by the page before its first run — on the declared values; a row that reads reference data refuses there by name. Written to target/readers, or --out; nothing committed.

commands.name: kit
commands.what: The tool as each person gets it: the two release-built programs beside exactly the files they read — the design among them as its files, design/ — with START_HERE.md and VERSION (and start.sh off Windows, where the daemon ships as Start VLEO.exe), in dist/vleo-<version>/. Zip it and share it; see docs/SHARING.md. --files-only leaves the programs out: the files the Python package carries.

commands.name: derisk
commands.what: Write the de-risking narrative — docs/DERISK_NARRATIVE.md and docs/derisking.csv — from every node's `[[version]]` record and the risk register. Generated, never edited.

commands.name: release
commands.what: Set the workspace version and regenerate. `--check` refuses while the workspace says another version — the release pipeline runs it.

commands.name: ready
commands.what: Whether a person should be asked to look yet.

commands.name: codeowners
commands.what: Regenerate CODEOWNERS from areas/teams.toml, for code paths only.

commands.name: bundle
commands.what: `bundle verify` re-checks every published set's hashes. `bundle publish` publishes a new one, permanently.

commands.name: setup
commands.what: Point git at the project's hooks. Once per checkout.

commands.name: variables
commands.what: Write docs/VARIABLES.md — every variable, its unit, its range and why.

commands.name: run
commands.what: Evaluate a row and everything it needs. Always n ran, m blocked, with the blocked named. `--save` writes the run and its inputs as a result file; `--keep` keeps it in the results folder, once. A question already kept there is shown from its saved result; `--again` runs it anyway.

commands.name: sweep
commands.what: Sweep a declared input across a range. Refused points are recorded, never dropped. `--keep` and `--again` as for run.

commands.name: campaign
commands.what: The defaults, the saved case and each case file named, against one row.

commands.name: list
commands.what: The rows, with kind, owner and state.

commands.name: show
commands.what: A row's sheet, as the engine holds it.

commands.name: cases
commands.what: The case, how its inputs divide into customer and condition, and whether a case is saved.

commands.name: inputs
commands.what: Every input of the case as a CSV — group, id, value, unit, default and range — to fill in and pass back with --inputs. With --inputs, a file from an older version comes out in the current template.

commands.name: result
commands.what: A saved result shown as it was — nothing runs. Reads a result's folder, the CSV `run --save` writes, or the report page it rides in; `--html` writes that report, to send. Given a results file (.vleor), lists the results it holds.

commands.name: results
commands.what: Saved results, many in one file to send or keep: every result in the results folder, or the ones named. Each goes out whole, and every value again as a row that Python (`vleo.results`) or any SQL reader can ask for.

commands.name: results
commands.what: The results in a results file, put back in the results folder exactly as they were — nothing runs. A question already kept is kept once.

commands.name: figure
commands.what: The numbers one figure of the solar-weather record draws, as the JSON its panel reads — the same function as `/v1/figures/solar/<id>`, on the same bundle and saved case. From Python, `vleo.figure(id, **params)` returns the same as a dict. An unknown id or key is refused by name, with a failing exit status.

commands.name: health
commands.what: Where exactly the design breaks, from one run of the whole design: every row closes, fails, is refused, blocked (naming the row it waits on), unproven (its own cases not reproduced) or open; each group as bad as its worst row, and the spacecraft as bad as its worst group. `--trace` walks one closure down to the rows that cause it — refused, open, unproven, or changed by a release taken into today's design — with their group and owner, and ranks the declared inputs it reads by how far each moves its margin, with the value that would make it close. Over the values still open behind it, it says whether the closure holds for all of their range, part of it or none of it, ranks them in a tornado, and names the least mature value it rests on. No closure is judged tight until the programme declares a margin policy, and it says so.

commands.name: selftest
commands.what: Check every fixture declaration in the tree is sound. `cargo test` executes them.

commands.name: data
commands.what: Fill the local reference-data store, say what is in it, or re-check its hashes.

commands.name: version
commands.what: The kernel, graph and build identity, and which graph the engine runs — the one read from the design's files, or today's design from a drive, with the releases it took. Then the design it runs and what it answers, each by its fingerprint: two computers that print the same two run the same design and give every answer alike, to the last bit, which CI checks on Linux, Windows and macOS. Every command that runs the engine opens the design first and refuses, saying why, when it does not open.

routes.what: This page.
The page's stylesheet.
The page's modules, one per concern, served as they are written — no build step between the source and what runs.
The page's type, bundled with the tool (web/fonts, IBM Plex Mono under the SIL Open Font License): the page looks the same everywhere and fetches nothing to do it.
The engine's identity: the contract version it speaks, kernel, graph, row count and data versions.
Every row and group, with what the tree needs to draw itself.
A row's generated page.
A row, as the engine holds it.
A row's lesson — its `lesson.toml`, checked as the gate checks it — or `lesson: null` for a row with none. A lesson that fails its check is refused with the reasons.
This manual, with what is true of the running tool right now.

Evaluate a row on the saved case. `node`, and optionally `mode`, `set`, and `inputs=defaults` to run the declared defaults instead. With `reuse=1`, a question already kept in the results folder is answered from its saved result, named in `from_saved`; `again=1` runs it anyway.
The same as GET, with the parameters in the body.
Every input of the case — group, unit, default, range and the saved value — whether a case is saved, the current template, and what the last carry-over did to it.

The saved case as a CSV to keep, in the current template with the record of any carry-over; with `inputs=defaults` the blank template; with `backup=1` the file as it was before the tool last carried it over.
Read a case — `csv=` a file's text, or `set=<id>:<si>` pairs — and say what it sets and every row it refuses. Saves nothing.
Save a case, the same parameters as the check. All or nothing: a case with any refused row is not saved. Written outside the repository.
Remove the saved case: every input back to its default.

A row's lesson form, as one self-contained HTML file to fill anywhere, checked as it is typed by the gate's own lesson check. Writes nothing — a filled one is checked with `xtask lesson check`, and goes into the design with its group's release.
Every registered risk, where it stands and every node version that moved it — the conclusion the risk-register rows draw — and the version each recorded node is at.
Every result kept on this machine, newest first, and where they are kept.
One saved result, as it was: `name`. Nothing runs.
A saved result's CSV, to keep or send: `name`.
A saved sweep's points as CSV, to keep or send: `name`.
A saved result as a report page that reads without the tool, draws its sweep, and carries its CSVs: `name`.
One figure of every kind — line, scatter, bar, heatmap, animation, 3D scene — with illustrative numbers, as a result's `figures` carries them. What a face is built and checked against; not a result.

The numbers one figure of the solar-weather record states, worked out by the engine from the bundle it holds (`crates/vleo-modules/src/record.rs`): `density` — the correlation of F10.7 with Ap, their medians, the share of days below both, and the F10.7 deciles that saw a storm day; `storm-scale` — days a year at G1 to G3 in each cycle, the busiest cycle and the largest Ap in each; `kp-ap` — the daily Ap at each worst three-hourly Kp and where the published table sits above it; `recurrence-f107` and `recurrence-ap` — the autocorrelation of the detrended record against lag under three windows, Bartlett's band and the rotation's peaks; `spikes` — the F10.7 spike threshold, the spike days and bursts, and their rate per thousand days of cycle phase. `mean-cycle` takes `v` (f107, ap or ssn) and `bins` (2 to 100): every cycle stacked on phase, the mean of the complete ones, and how well the last two complete cycles repeat each other. `segments` takes `v` (ap or f107): the histogram and each band's share, banded by the rows themselves (`sw_regime`, `sw_activity_band`), and where the record crosses each cut; `regime-phase` — the share of days at each cycle phase `sw_regime` calls storm, and quiet. `climate` takes `v` and `by` (year, doy or month): the record's mean in each group on its own calendar, and the mean over its days; `smoother` takes `v`: each month's mean beside the 13-month smoothed value from `monthly_means.csv`, and what the smoothing removes. `growth` takes `v` and `by` (all or cycle): the signed change over leads from 30 days to 15 years at the 50th, 90th, 95th and 99th percentiles with the pairs behind each, or the 95th within each cycle. `forecast` takes `view` (lead, year or age): the issued 27-day outlook's skill against persistence — from the day before the issue, and from the issue date itself, which leaks — its bias and RMS error at each lead from 1 to 27 or in each year of issue on leads 1 to 14, with the pairs behind each; or the gaps between one issue and the next. `drivers` — the solar crossing's twenty-five scenario cells run on the saved case against the legacy tool's own run of them (`matlab/reference/mission_drivers.csv`): each ratio and gap, where each quantity's gap is widest, how many cells agree to a tenth of a per cent, and how far the worst is out. `thermosphere` takes `view` (solar, kp, slot or shape): env_exospheric_temperature run and probed as the panel asks — the three ways to raise the flux and their slopes, one Kp curve per scenario at its own flux with its two Kp readings and the widest gap, each scenario's two readings side by side, or the Kp sweep against the straight line its quiet end sets. `design` takes `v` (ap or f107): for Ap, with `g` (1 to 3) and `req` (l3_solar_req_03, _04 or _05), sw_storm_return_level swept over the mission duration, the G-level bound and the requirement, where the curve first reaches each, and the record's days at or above the bound in how many runs; for F10.7, with `reqf` (l3_solar_req_01 or _02), the four design-window rows and the analogue's peak swept the same way, the worst single day and what is left of the requirement above it, the window's width and where the peak first climbs above the hot single day. `closure` takes `pair` (01 to 05): the decision that spends that closure's margin fastest, by the levers' own ranking with the requirement skipped, the margin and the achieved quantity swept over it, and where each runs out. In these two the sweeps and the ranking run on the case the request carries, `set=` overrides and all, and each row's own answer — the requirement, the achieved margin — on the saved case, as the page's engine values are. The page draws them and computes none; an id the engine does not work out is refused by name.

Run, and keep what it returned and the inputs it ran on as a result folder: the parameters of `/v1/run`, and `label`; with `over`, `from`, `to` and `points` the sweep is kept with it. Kept once: a question already kept answers `already` and names it. Written outside the repository.
Keep a result somebody sent: `csv=` its CSV or the text of its report, and `sweep=` its sweep CSV when it is one. Kept once, as a save is.

Keep every result a results file (`results.vleor`) holds: `vleor=` the file, base64. Each is kept once, as a save is, pinned where the file says so; the answer names each one, how many were new and how many already kept.
Pin a saved result so every value is kept for good (`on=1`), or unpin it (`on=0`) so it is thinned to its summary once it is older than `VLEO_KEEP_DAYS`: `name`.
Remove one saved result: `name`.
Make a saved result's inputs the case: `name`. Checked like any case, and refused whole if one cannot apply.
A behaviour sweep, as `vleo sweep`. Refused points are reported with their reason. `reuse=1` and `again=1` as for `/v1/run`.
One relation at chosen inputs: `node`, and `in=<var>:<value>` for each. Answers even where a run would refuse a supplied value.
Which declared decisions actually move a row's answer, and by how much: `node`.
The largest fully-published branches a row is part of: `node`.
A reference-data set's published files.
The published output of the tool this was ported from, for comparison.

env.name: VLEO_CASE
env.what: Where the saved case is kept — the CSV the Inputs page and `vleo run` read. Outside the repository, so git never sees it. A copy made before a carry-over sits beside it.

env.name: VLEO_CONTRACT_RECORD
env.what: Set to `1` when running the contract tests, to record contract/examples/ again from the real engine after an answer's shape changes, and draft a schema for a route that has none. It never rewrites a schema. Unset, the tests only check.

env.name: VLEO_BASELINE
env.what: Set to `write` when running the test of today's answers, to record baseline/today.csv again after a deliberate change to the design, in the same commit as the change. Unset, the test compares and fails on any difference.

env.name: VLEO_KINDS
env.what: Set to `write` when running the tests of crates/vleo-kinds, to write the table of file kinds into the Python reader (crates/vleo-py/python/vleo/files.py) again after a deliberate change to the table. Unset, the test compares and fails on any difference.

env.name: VLEO_BROWSER_ANSWERS
env.what: The file `tools/readers_check.py --answers` wrote: every answer the engine in a readers' page gave. Set when running `cargo test -- --include-ignored` in crates/vleo-kernel-wasm, it holds each of those answers to the same engine built natively, byte for byte. Unset, that one test refuses to run and says why; the pipeline's readers job sets it.
env.default: unset — the comparison is not run

env.name: VLEO_LOG
env.what: Where a crash log is written when the tool hits a bug — one small text file per bug, naming the line of code; the newest 50 are kept. Send the file to whoever maintains the tool. Set but empty counts as unset.

env.name: VLEO_RESULTS
env.what: Where saved results are kept, one folder each — the Results page and `vleo run --keep`. Outside the repository. Point it at a shared or synced folder and everyone keeps one archive: each question is kept once, a question a colleague answered is shown rather than run again, and every result is written whole. Set but empty counts as unset.

env.name: VLEO_KEEP_DAYS
env.what: How many days a saved result keeps every value. When the daemon starts, an unpinned result older than this is thinned to its summary — the inputs it ran on, its answer, what could not run — and says so; a pinned one is kept whole for good. `0` never thins. A folder named by `VLEO_RESULTS` — usually the shared archive — is kept whole unless this is set too: thinning it is everyone's decision, not whichever laptop starts first. A value that is not a whole number of days thins nothing and says why.
env.default: 30; kept whole when VLEO_RESULTS names the folder

env.name: VLEO_ROOT
env.what: Where the daemon finds the web face, the tree and its pages. Unset, it looks upward from where it was started, then from beside its own program — which is how a kit runs with no checkout.

env.name: VLEO_DESIGN
env.what: A folder of the design's files for the daemon to read the design from, in place of design/ beside it: its group, node and case files, read as the folders they came from. A name that is not a folder, a folder that does not open, and a file in it written by a newer application than the daemon each stop the daemon, naming why: it never falls back to whatever sits beside it.
env.default: design/ beside the tool, else the folders

env.name: VLEO_DRIVE
env.what: A shared drive to build today's design from: every group's latest sealed release in its `groups/<group>/releases/` that passes its checks — its seal, its content, and each node checked against the design — taken into the design, in memory. A group whose latest is refused is built from its last good release, and the tool says which release each group's part is, and why one was refused. A folder that is not a drive stops the tool, naming why. Nothing on the drive is written.
env.default: unset: the design's files, as they are

env.name: VLEO_PORT
env.what: The first port the daemon tries. It takes the first free one of sixteen from there.

env.name: VLEO_DATA
env.what: Where the local reference-data store lives.

env.name: VLEO_DAEMON
env.what: Where the checking scripts in tools/ find a running daemon.

env.name: VLEO_CHROMIUM
env.what: The browser the panel check drives, when it cannot find the installed one on its own.

cannot.what: Change a node — any field of its sheet
cannot.why: A change to the design has to be checked against every row that reads it, implemented, given evidence and released, so that everyone runs the same thing.
cannot.instead: Its node engineer changes it in the node's own file; it arrives with the group's sealed release.

cannot.why: A new node is a new node file in the tree with an owner, a place among its siblings and interfaces to rows that exist.
cannot.instead: Its subsystem engineer adds it to the group, and it arrives with the group's sealed release.

cannot.why: Other rows read it. Removing one is a change to what every reader of it computes, and is decided in review.
cannot.instead: Its subsystem engineer retires it in the group's release, after `cargo run -p xtask -- reach` shows what reads it.

cannot.what: Move a node, rename it, or change its owner, layer, kind or order
cannot.why: These move the tree or change who reviews the row. Its identifier is also its file and its variable name.
cannot.instead: Its subsystem engineer changes it in the group's release (docs/GROUP_APPS.md); the reason for each is under Reference.

cannot.what: Change a declared number in the design itself
cannot.why: A what-if and the saved case never touch the sheet: a declared value carries the name of the person who chose it.
cannot.instead: For your own runs, the case. For the design's default, the node's own file.

cannot.why: An expected value may never come from the code under test. Only a person records one, with its source.
cannot.instead: The node engineer adds it to their node's file in their group's application, with the value's source and provenance.

cannot.what: Put your name against a relation
cannot.why: Signing is an act of reading the relation against its source, done by the person who owns it.
cannot.instead: The node engineer signs their node's file in their group's application (docs/GROUP_APPS.md).

cannot.what: Run the checks, the tests or the generators for the whole tree
cannot.why: They are what decides whether a change may be merged, so they run where the change is committed — and in the pipeline, on every push.
cannot.instead: cargo run -p xtask -- gate && cargo test

fields.ask: what is the declared number

fields.ask: why is it this relation and not another

fields.ask: how should the answer be read

fields.ask: where does the simple version stop being true

fields.ask: your code — the implementation you wrote and tested, pasted whole

fields.ask: your test code — the script that ran your code on each test case and printed the results

fields.ask: where and how you ran it: the tool and its version, the machine, the date

arrays.name: input
arrays.label: what this row reads
arrays.why: the consumer declares what it expects, and assembly refuses a mismatch against what the producer publishes. It is also the derivation graph: an input is an edge, and the edges are what decide what runs before what

arrays.name: algorithm
arrays.label: the steps
arrays.why: each step becomes one numbered hole in the generated model, and the hole is where a person writes the few typed lines that compose relations from the kernel. The step's text is the comment above it

arrays.name: theory
arrays.label: how the relation was arrived at
arrays.why: the expression says what the relation is; these say how it was got to. A relation an assistant invented carries a citation just as convincingly, and the derivation is what a reviewer reads instead of taking the citation's word

arrays.name: assumption
arrays.label: what has to be true for this to hold
arrays.why: an assumption nobody wrote down is one nobody can check. Each says what it assumes AND the case it fails in, because an assumption with no failure case is a sentence rather than a warning

arrays.name: risk
arrays.label: the risks this row registers
arrays.why: a risk is registered once, here, and moved only by node versions — a risk is reduced because something was tested, and the version that tested it is the record of how. Which risk-register row holds a risk says what kind it is

arrays.name: case
arrays.label: your test cases
arrays.why: inputs and the answer YOUR code gave, or that your code refuses them. They decide: the method is run on each one before you send the form, and the code the tool generates must reproduce every one before the node is connected to anything. At least three answers and one refusal

arrays.name: flight
arrays.label: flight software kept with this node
arrays.why: on-board code that implements this node, stored with its test beside the relation it implements, so the two are reviewed and versioned together
